name: Ni vs -na- (is vs has)
explanation: This deck contrasts two common Swahili patterns that can both sound like simple English sentences with "is" or "has". Ni is a copula: it identifies or classifies something, like "is", "am", or "are". The -na- pattern is part of a verb form. With verbs like kuwa na, it expresses possession: ana maji means "he/she has water", and ina maji means "it has water". With other verbs, -na- can simply mark present tense, as in inamaanisha, "it means". Watch the subject prefix before -na-: a-na for a person, i-na for many class 9 nouns or hii, and so on.

cards.explanation: Use ni when you are identifying what something is. Hii ni maji means you are saying "this thing equals water" or "this is water".
Use ina when the subject has something. Hii ina maji means "this has water". The i- prefix agrees with hii here, and -na- carries the possession idea.
Ni classifies or identifies the thing. The sentence says that this object is a bottle, not that it contains or owns a bottle.
Chupa is the subject, and ina shows possession or containment: the bottle has water in it. This is different from Chupa ni maji, which would mean "the bottle is water".
Ni can also connect a subject with a description. Hii ni nzuri means "this is good". The adjective nzuri describes what this thing is like.
Inamaanisha contains -na-, but here it is not possession. It is the present-tense part of the verb maanisha, "to mean". So the sentence asks "What does this mean?"
This phrase is built from ina plus maana, "meaning". Literally it is close to "it has meaning", but naturally it means "it means".
Ana is used with a human singular subject: a-na. Mtoto ana maji means "the child has water".
This uses ni because the sentence describes what the child is like. Mzuri agrees with mtoto as a person-class adjective.
Here ina maana can be understood more literally as "this has meaning". The same words often function naturally as "this means" depending on context.
